source.title_on_document: Can LLMs Generate Novel Research Ideas? A Large-Scale Human Study with 100+ NLP Researchers

supplement.where: Appendices A to Y are in this PDF (pp. 26-94). The agent code and all human review scores are released at https://github.com/NoviScl/AI-Researcher (p. 1, footnote 1).
supplement.holds: Appendix N, Table 17 (p. 47): linear mixed-effects coefficients with standard errors for all five metrics (topic random effects, reviewer and idea variance components). Appendix O, Figure 5 (p. 48): scores by topic, figure only. Appendix I, Table 12 (p. 42): overlap of the two AI conditions. Appendix J (p. 42): honor code and the one excluded human idea. Appendices K to M, Tables 13-16 (pp. 43-45): participant positions and institutions. Appendix E (pp. 32-35): review form and scale anchors.

paper_design_summary: The study analyzed ideas from 49 NLP researchers who each wrote one proposal under an honor code forbidding AI tools, after one of 50 submitted ideas was excluded (p. 7; Appendix J, p. 42). A claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 agent generated topic-matched proposals, ranked either by the agent or by the first author; all conditions received LLM style normalization before 79 researchers supplied 298 unique blind reviews of novelty, excitement, feasibility, expected effectiveness, and overall merit on 1-10 scales (pp. 4-9). This is an AI-versus-human output comparison, with no random assignment of writers to AI assistance (pp. 4-5, 8, 42).

studies.label: Human study: expert-written versus AI-agent research ideas, blind expert review

assignment.what_was_assigned: No writer was assigned to AI assistance. The three conditions are sources of ideas: human experts, the AI agent, and the AI agent with the first author's reranking. For each topic a human writer chose, the agent generated a matching AI idea. In the human study, reviewers were randomly assigned to ideas within their preferred topics, with ideas from each condition balanced for each reviewer.
assignment.quote: We then randomly assign them to ideas within their selected topics and all ideas are anonymized. In the assignment, we balance the number of ideas from each condition for each reviewer
assignment.locator: p. 8, Section 4.4 (Review Assignment); topic matching p. 4, Section 2; conditions pp. 4-5, Section 2
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 18, Section 10 and footnote 12 (https://osf.io/z6qa4): the preregistration covers a planned follow-up comparing AI ideas with EMNLP 2024 accepted papers, not this human study.

arms.name: Human Ideas
arms.description: Ideas from 49 analyzed expert NLP writers, each instructed to write one idea within 10 days without AI tools; one of 50 submitted ideas was excluded. All retained ideas were style-normalized by an LLM before review (pp. 4, 7; Appendix J, p. 42).

arms.name: AI Ideas
arms.description: Top-ranked project proposals from the LLM ideation agent (retrieval, 4000 seed ideas per topic, deduplication, Swiss-system pairwise ranking by Claude-3.5-Sonnet); 49 ideas topic-matched to the human ideas. No people produce these.

arms.name: AI Ideas + Human Rerank
arms.description: Proposals from the same LLM agent, with the top ideas selected manually by the paper's first author instead of the LLM ranker; 49 ideas. No people produce these.

participants.exclusions: Appendix J reports 50 submitted human ideas, one per writer, and one excluded as essentially a paraphrase of an existing paper's abstract, leaving 49 writers analyzed (p. 7; Appendix J, p. 42). The excluded participant was compensated but excluded from the review task (p. 42). Separately, 79 reviewers, 24 of whom also wrote ideas, produced 298 unique reviews; the paper reports 104 people across the two tasks (p. 7). Reviewers are outcome assessors and are not added to the analyzed creative-task participant count. The AI conditions contain model-generated ideas, not additional participant arms.
participants.who: Analyzed idea writers: 49 NLP researchers screened for at least one paper at a major AI venue (p. 7): 36 PhD students, 9 Master's, 1 undergraduate, 1 postdoc, 1 research scientist, 1 ML engineer (Table 13, p. 43), from 26 institutions (Table 15, p. 44). Reviewers: 79 NLP researchers: 63 PhD, 7 postdoc, 5 Master's, 3 research scientists, 1 ML engineer (Table 14, p. 43), from 32 institutions (Table 16, p. 45).
participants.country: United States (p. 7, footnote 6: 'We have to recruit participants located in the US due to logistical reasons.'). Table 15 nonetheless lists some non-US institutions (University of Toronto, National University of Singapore, Peking University, Tsinghua University; p. 44).
participants.quote: We collected N =50 ideas originally and manually checked all of them for quality control. We filtered out one of them as being essentially a paraphrase of an existing paper’s abstract.
participants.locator: p. 42, Appendix J (submitted ideas and exclusion); p. 7, Section 4.1 (49 writers analyzed and separate reviewer counts); Tables 13-16, pp. 43-45

ai_tool.name_model: LLM ideation agent with claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 as backbone (p. 5, Section 3.1); Claude-3.5-Sonnet zero-shot pairwise ranker (p. 6, Section 3.3)
ai_tool.how_used: The AI generates ideas on its own: it retrieves papers through the Semantic Scholar API, generates 4000 seed ideas per topic, deduplicates them with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings (cosine threshold 0.8), expands them into full proposals, filters about 1 percent of proposals on novelty and feasibility checks (p. 36), and ranks them in a Swiss-system pairwise tournament with N = 5 rounds (p. 6). Human writers were instructed not to use AI tools while writing ideas (Appendix J, p. 42). All ideas, human and AI, passed through an LLM style-normalization prompt (Appendix D, p. 31) before review.

task.description: Write one research idea (project proposal) on novel prompting methods in one of seven NLP topics (Bias, Coding, Safety, Multilingual, Factuality, Math, Uncertainty), following a fixed template: title, problem statement, motivation, proposed method, step-by-step experiment plan, test case examples, fallback plan (pp. 3-4, Appendices A-C).
task.duration: Writers had 10 days per idea and reported 5.5 hours on average (p. 7; Table 3, p. 8). Reviewers had one week and spent 31.7 minutes per review on average (p. 7; Table 6, p. 9).

outcomes.name: Novelty score (1-10)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Blind review by NLP researchers on a 1-10 scale with anchors; the form defines novelty as 'Whether the idea is creative and different from existing works on the topic, and brings fresh insights' (Appendix E, p. 32). Four analyses of the same ratings: Test 1, each review a datapoint, two-tailed Welch t-tests with Bonferroni correction (Table 7, p. 10; per-condition sizes 119, 109, 109 reviews); Test 2, idea-level means, 49 ideas per condition (Table 8, p. 11); Test 3, within-reviewer mean differences, one-sample t-tests with Bonferroni correction (Table 9, p. 12); linear mixed-effects model with topic random intercepts and slopes and reviewer and idea variance components (Table 17, p. 47). Topic breakdown in Figure 5 (p. 48), figure only.

contrasts.reported: Test 1 (reviews): Human Ideas 4.84 (SD 1.79, SE 0.16, n = 119) vs AI Ideas 5.64 (SD 1.76, SE 0.17, n = 109), p = 0.00** (Welch, Bonferroni). Test 2 (ideas): Human 4.86 (SD 1.26, SE 0.18, n = 49) vs AI 5.62 (SD 1.39, SE 0.20, n = 49), p = 0.03*. Test 3 (reviewers): N = 70, mean diff 0.94, p = 0.00**. Mixed model: Condition[AI Ideas] 0.756 (SE 0.331), p = 0.023*; intercept 4.826 (SE 0.217). The Appendix N text cites this coefficient as 0.761 (p. 46).

studies.label: Model-only analysis: duplication among the agent's seed ideas (Section 7.1)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing; no people. The LLM agent generated 4000 seed ideas per topic, and the authors measured how many were non-duplicates as generation continued.
assignment.quote: To answer this question, we take a closer look at 4000 generated seed ideas for each topic.

arms.name: AI seed ideas
arms.description: Seed ideas generated by the claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 agent, 4000 per topic, with the titles of all earlier ideas appended to the prompt to ask the model to avoid repetitions (p. 6).

ai_tool.name_model: claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620 agent; similarity computed with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Sentence-Transformers)
ai_tool.how_used: Autonomous seed-idea generation; retrieval augmentation applied half of the time (Appendix F, p. 36); titles of all previously generated ideas appended to the prompt to discourage repetition (p. 6).

task.description: Generate seed research ideas on the seven prompting topics.

outcomes.name: Share of non-duplicate seed ideas as generation scales
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Each raw seed idea is encoded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (Sentence-Transformers) and compared by cosine similarity with all previously generated ideas on the same topic; an idea counts as a duplicate if its similarity with any earlier idea is above 0.8 (p. 13). Figure 4 (p. 14) plots the percentage of non-duplicates in each new batch and the accumulated non-duplicates over 4000 seed ideas per topic, with all data points averaged across topics; no uncertainty is reported. This is redundancy within one model's outputs, not diversity across people, so diversity_detail stays empty.

contrasts.treatment_arm: Later batches of generated seed ideas
contrasts.control_arm: Earlier batches of generated seed ideas
contrasts.reported: The percentage of non-duplicates in newly generated batches keeps decreasing and the accumulated non-duplicates plateau; 'out of the 4000 generated seed ideas, there are only 200 non-duplicate unique ideas' (pp. 13-14). Figure 4 caption: 'All data points are averaged across all topics.' Section 3.2 says deduplication leaves about 5% non-duplicated ideas (p. 6).

eligibility.reason: For the saved arXiv v1, criterion 1 is not met: human-written ideas are compared with autonomous AI-generated ideas (with or without the first author's reranking), and reviewers, not writers receiving AI assistance, were randomly assigned (pp. 4-5, Section 2; p. 8, Section 4.4; Appendix J, p. 42). Criterion 2 is independently not met: 49 idea writers were analyzed after one of 50 submitted ideas was excluded, just below the 50-person threshold (p. 7, Section 4.1; Appendix J, p. 42). The 79 reviewers and the reported 104 people across writing and reviewing do not constitute 104 creative-task participants, and model-generated ideas do not add people (p. 7). Criterion 3 is met: blinded experts scored novelty on the written proposals using a 1-10 scale explicitly assessing creativity and differences from existing work (p. 4, Review and Evaluation; Appendix E, p. 32, item 9). Style normalization of all conditions before review does not create a randomized AI-assistance contrast (p. 4; Appendix D, p. 31). S2 is model-only and adds no human participants (pp. 13-14, Section 7.1). The unverified possibility of a later version with different analyzed counts is recorded in final.open_items; the decision here concerns the saved PDF.

one_line_finding: Expert reviewers rated the LLM agent's research ideas more novel than ideas from 49 analyzed NLP writers (review level: AI 5.64 and AI + Human Rerank 5.81 vs Human 4.84, p < 0.01, Table 7, p. 10; idea level: 5.62 and 5.78 vs 4.86, p < 0.05, Table 8, p. 11; mixed model 0.756, SE 0.331, Table 17, p. 47), with no significant difference in feasibility (6.34 and 6.44 vs 6.61, Table 7).
open_questions: The Overall score (S1-O5) is coded 'other' as a conference-acceptance merit rating; a reviewer could argue for overall_creativity or usefulness.
Human ideas were rewritten for style by an LLM before review (p. 4; Appendix D, p. 31), so the human-arm outputs passed through AI editing; the first author checked that content was preserved.

Per-condition review counts in Table 7 (119 + 109 + 109 = 337) exceed the 298 unique reviews stated on pp. 7 and 9. Ideas shared by the two AI conditions may explain it, but the paper does not say so.
The overlap between AI Ideas and AI Ideas + Human Rerank is 17 of 49 in the text (pp. 7, 42), but the Total row of Table 12 shows 18 overlap and 31 new (p. 42).
The Appendix N text cites mixed-model coefficients of 0.761 for novelty and -0.330 for feasibility (p. 46), while Table 17 prints 0.756 and -0.300 (p. 47). This record uses Table 17.
The file is arXiv v1 of 6 Sep 2024 and the library file name says 2025; a later version may report different counts and should be checked before extraction.
notes: n_units = 298 for the S1 outcomes is the stated count of unique reviews (pp. 7, 9); every review scores all five metrics, and Table 7's per-condition sizes are 119, 109, and 109. Outcomes not coded as separate records: Figure 5 topic breakdown (robustness variant, p. 48, figure only); idea length in words (Table 3, p. 8: Human 901.7, AI 1186.3, AI + Human Rerank 1174.0, measured after style normalization, descriptive only); inter-reviewer agreement of 56.1 percent (Section 6.3, p. 13; Table 11, p. 14); LLM-as-judge agreement with human reviewers (Table 11, p. 14), which scores evaluators, not ideas; metric correlations (Table 10, p. 13); execution-agent success rates (Appendix Y, Table 18, p. 93). Post-study self-report: 37 of the 49 analyzed writers came up with the idea on the spot, and writers placed their idea at about the top 43 percent of their past ideas (p. 12, Section 6.1). A small human study found 50 percent accuracy in telling AI from human ideas after style normalization (p. 4). Within the paper, 24 of the 79 reviewers also wrote ideas, and no reviewer reviewed their own idea (p. 7). The analyzed creative-task sample is 49 idea writers; the 79 reviewers and reported 104 people across the two tasks are recorded separately (p. 7; Appendix J, p. 42). Finalization: the entire markdown conversion, including Appendices A-Y, was read, and the recorded numerical results and eligibility passages were checked against PDF text. No c022.*.json challenge files were present, and reconciliation.differences contains no unresolved items. The challenge-resolution counts are therefore zero; updates to counts prose and the eligibility explanation are spec clarifications, not checker resolutions. The six original open_questions are assessed individually in final.open_items. source.supplement was already complete and was confirmed against the saved PDF.

open_items.item: Overall score coding: retain other because Appendix E, item 17 (p. 34), uses conference-acceptance and overall-merit anchors. No additional material is needed for eligibility: the separately defined novelty score explicitly assesses creative, different ideas (Appendix E, item 9, p. 32), so criterion 3 is met regardless of the overall-score label.

LLM style normalization of human ideas: confirmed for all conditions before review (p. 4; Appendix D, p. 31). The first author reports checking preservation of content (p. 4); human writers were instructed not to use AI (Appendix J, p. 42). This preprocessing is not random assignment of writers to AI assistance, so no additional material is needed to determine criterion 1.

Review counts: Table 7 (p. 10) gives 119, 109, and 109 reviews by condition, whereas Sections 4.1 and 4.4 (pp. 7, 9) report 298 unique reviews. The PDF does not reconcile these counts; retain 298 as unique reviews and retain the printed condition sizes. Posted review-level data with idea identifiers and condition membership would establish whether shared AI ideas cause reviews to enter both AI conditions. These are ratings, not creative-task participant counts, so no eligibility criterion changes.

AI-condition overlap: prose reports 17 shared and 32 different ideas (pp. 7, 42), but Table 12 reports 18 shared and 31 new (p. 42). Posted idea identifiers and condition membership would settle the discrepancy. These are model-generated ideas, not additional people, so no eligibility criterion changes.

Mixed-model coefficients: Appendix N prose (p. 46) gives 0.761 for novelty and -0.330 for feasibility; Table 17 (p. 47) gives 0.756 and -0.300. Retain the table values with their printed standard errors and flag the conflict. Author confirmation of the intended estimates and analysis would settle it. This concerns effect estimates, not assignment, analyzed people, or whether novelty was scored on outputs.

Later-version analyzed writer count: the saved document is arXiv v1 of 6 Sep 2024 (p. 1), despite 2025 in its library filename. A later published version, if one exists, must be checked for its analyzed writer count and exclusions because the saved version has 49 analyzed writers (p. 7; Appendix J, p. 42), just below the criterion 2 threshold. This could affect criterion 2 for an updated record; it does not make the saved version's nonrandomized AI-versus-human design eligible. No later version has been verified in this finalization.
